title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 6: e-Values for the e-Age and Beyond
keywords: e-Values for the e-Age and Beyond
Who am I? Why was I born?
the farmer and the horse (Good luck? Bad luck?)
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's address at a CAP forum honoring President Sergio Osmena, arguing that the four fundamental questions of being and living are answered not by carnal satisfactions but by values, and that three in particular -- excellence, ethics and eternity -- are the immutable 'e-values for the e-age and beyond.'

His tribute to CAP chairman Dr. Alejandro R. Roces, his FEU mentor, adviser of the National Union of Students he organized in 1957, his wedding sponsor in 1961 and, as education secretary under President Macapagal, the man who made the newly admitted lawyer his legal counsel.

His diagnosis of Philippine duplicity -- leaders who keep double standards, double speak and spin doctors, and a 90-percent Christian nation leading dichotomized lives -- as the cause of a country that is among the poorest, most graft-ridden and most violent in the region, curable only by a change in leaders from the inside out.

His account of eternity as the final destiny: spiritual laws with real consequences, the Ten Commandments as negative directions and the Beatitudes as positive ones, a plea addressed equally to Muslim, Jewish and other God-loving listeners, and Vaclav Havel's testimony to the common elements underlying most religions and cultures.
sub_topics: He opened by saying the guest speaker should have been Dr. Alejandro R. Roces himself, whom he first met over forty years ago when Roces was dean of FEU's Institute of Arts and Sciences and taught that the educated person is the cultured person.

He recounted Roces's role in his life: benefactor and coach in campus leadership battles, adviser he recruited in 1957 for the National Union of Students, wedding sponsor in 1961 (hence 'Ninong Anding'), and, as Macapagal's education secretary, the official who appointed the year-old lawyer as his legal counsel.

He turned to a televised biography of Aristotle Onassis -- the Greek shipping tycoon, husband of Jacqueline Kennedy, companion of Maria Callas, courted by heads of state -- who nonetheless died a broken man in 1975 without answers to the fundamental questions.

He posed those four questions -- Who am I? Why was I born? Where am I headed for? How do I get there? -- and warned that without answers life becomes endless journeys of ups and downs without vision, of gluttony without wellness, of chasing carnal pleasures without catching lasting joy.

He argued that humans are rational beings who share animal needs, but that ultimate fulfillment depends on their rationality and divinity, not their carnality, and defined values as the traits born of man's higher self that elevate him from mere existence to life on high.

On the first value, excellence, he defined it as competence, dedication to duty and hard work put together, not confined to scholarly pursuits but owed by teachers, soldiers, lawyers, programmers and plain ordinary workers alike.

He illustrated excellence with the tradespeople he patronizes -- Larry the blind masseur who presses the right muscle with the right pressure, his favorite barber and his old tailor -- who are not the cheapest but are kept going by esteem for their expertise as much as by payment.
He repeated that for the truly educated, excellence means both appreciation of the arts, history, literature and humanities and mastery of a specialized discipline.

On hard work he cited Toribio Teodoro, Gandhi and Edison's line about ninety-nine percent perspiration, and the Asiaweek interview with Diosdado 'Dado' Banatao of Iguig, said by UP President Francisco Nemenzo to be richer than the Ayalas, whose secret was 'hard work' and who counted 100 or 200 failures for every success.

He told the medieval parable of the farmer whose runaway horse, ten returned horses, son's broken leg and exemption from a lost war each drew the same reply -- 'Good luck? Bad luck? Who knows? I will just keep on doing my best' -- and applied it to events outside our control.
He quoted St. Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians on being afflicted but not crushed, persecuted but never abandoned, struck down but never destroyed.

On ethics he rooted the value in personal integrity understood as honesty and truth, acting in accordance with what is true regardless of personal consequences, which requires moral courage, purity of spirit and clarity of conscience.

He pointed to professional canons and, for government leaders, to Republic Act No. 6713 and its declaration that public officials must be accountable, act with patriotism and justice, lead modest lives and uphold public interest over private interest.

He charged that society has bastardized ethics into public relations techniques -- double standards for kin and friends, double speak, spin doctors, ghost-written orators, almsgivers of crumbs from ill-gotten money, model spouses with several lovers -- and called duplicity the opposite of integrity and a malaise that subverts the national character.

He asked why a country of theoretically unassailable institutions and more than 90 percent Christians is among the poorest, most graft-ridden and most violent, citing the Catholic Church's answer that Christians lead dichotomized lives -- Christians in faith but not in deeds, inside churches but not in offices.

He prescribed a return to old-fashioned ethical values and a change in leaders from the inside out, embracing head, heart, hands and feet -- to know what must be reformed, to will the change, and to implement it.

On eternity he repeated the parallel of spiritual laws with civil, criminal and physical laws, distinguished the Ten Commandments as negative directions from the Beatitudes as positive pronouncements, and addressed the same plea to Muslim, Jewish and other God-loving listeners since every religion recognizes an eternal Power.

He quoted Vaclav Havel on the common elements at the foundation of most religions and cultures, and argued that without faith in a Transcendental Being civilizations collapse and humans become no different from animals ruling by might and not by right.
He added transparency as a fourth value for government leaders -- no private deals, no under-the-table transactions -- but set it aside because most of the forum were not public servants.

In his epilogue he welcomed the e-age of e-commerce, e-health, e-media, e-medicine and e-law while advocating the old e-values as timeless, and answered his four opening questions: we are children of one God, born to love, honor and obey Him, headed for reunion with Him, reaching it by practising excellence, ethics and eternity daily.

stances.claim: Satisfying only our carnal and sensual natures leaves us afflicted and broken, because ultimate joy depends on fulfilling our rational and divine natures, which is what values do.
stances.rhetorical_move: cautionary biography then anthropology: Onassis's wealth and broken death, followed by a definition of values as traits of man's higher self

stances.claim: Excellence is not confined to scholarly pursuits: it is competence, dedication to duty and hard work owed by every worker, and the truly educated person combines the humanities with a specialty.
stances.rhetorical_move: everyday illustration -- the blind masseur, the barber, the tailor -- generalized to doctors, lawyers and public servants

stances.claim: Adversities and misfortunes are often preludes to greater victory, so one should keep doing one's best whatever happens.
stances.rhetorical_move: parable of the medieval farmer with its refrain, reinforced by St. Paul's afflicted-but-not-crushed passage

stances.claim: The Philippines is poor, graft-ridden and violent despite unassailable institutions because its Christians and its leaders lead dichotomized, duplicitous lives, and the cure is a change in leaders from the inside out.
stances.rhetorical_move: diagnostic question and answer, borrowing the Catholic Church's explanation and restating it in secular language

stances.claim: Every religion recognizes an eternal Power greater than ourselves, and without belief in transcendence civilizations and cultures will collapse.
stances.rhetorical_move: ecumenical widening plus an outside authority (Havel) on the common elements beneath religions and cultures

notable_anecdotes: He recalled inviting Dr. Roces in 1957 to advise the National Union of Students he had helped organize, esteeming him so much that he and his wife asked him to be their wedding sponsor in 1961, thereafter calling him Ninong Anding.
He recalled that Roces, as Macapagal's education secretary, appointed him legal counsel and entrusted him with delicate responsibilities although he had passed the bar only the previous year.

He described watching a televised biography of Aristotle Onassis, who brushed shoulders with heads of state and married Jacqueline Kennedy yet died a broken man in 1975 without love, peace or fulfillment.

He told of rewarding his tired body each weekend with a massage from Larry, a blind masseur who has mastered the art, and of paying his favorite barber and old tailor generously because they value the esteem given their expertise.

He retold the medieval parable of the farmer whose neighbors called each turn good or bad luck -- the lost horse, the ten horses, the son's broken leg, the war that spared him -- while the farmer answered only that he would keep doing his best.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' reproduced CJP's address to a CAP forum honoring President Sergio Osmena, which he began by insisting the speaker should have been his host, Dr. Alejandro R. Roces -- his FEU mentor, the adviser he recruited for the National Union of Students in 1957, his wedding sponsor in 1961, and the education secretary who made him his legal counsel a year after he passed the bar. He then recounted a televised biography of Aristotle Onassis, who commanded wealth, heads of state and famous women yet died a broken man in 1975 because he never answered the questions Who am I? Why was I born? Where am I headed for? How do I get there? Humans, he argued, share animal appetites but find fulfillment only in their rational and divine natures, and what we call values are the traits that lift us from mere existence to life on high. He then set out three: excellence, defined as competence, dedication to duty and hard work, illustrated by his blind masseur Larry, his barber and his tailor, by Edison's line on perspiration and by Dado Banatao's counting of 100 or 200 failures for every success, and taught by the parable of the farmer who met every turn of fortune with 'Good luck? Bad luck? Who knows?'; ethics, rooted in integrity as honesty and truth regardless of personal consequences, codified for officials in RA 6713 and betrayed by leaders' double standards, double speak and spin doctors, which he blamed, with the Catholic Church's diagnosis of dichotomized Christian lives, for the country's poverty, graft and violence; and eternity, where spiritual laws carry consequences as civil and physical laws do, a plea he extended to Muslim, Jewish and other God-loving listeners, supported by Havel on the common elements beneath religions. He added transparency as a fourth value for public servants, and closed by calling excellence, ethics and eternity the immutable e-values for the e-age and beyond.
